name: क्षेत्र-क्षेत्रज्ञविभागयोग
teaching: The body, the mind, desire, aversion, intelligence — all of it is the field. You are the knower of the field. Liberation begins with this clean distinction: whatever can be watched is not the watcher. The same light knows every field, undivided, like one sun illumining the whole world. One cut creates the chapter: the field, and its knower. Everything observable — body, mind, even feeling — is field; the seer is never the seen. Whoever holds that distinction, in any life, holds the door.
questions: List what you call 'me' — body, moods, history, opinions. Which of these can you observe? What is left?
Krishna defines knowledge as humility, harmlessness, steadiness. Where has your knowledge made you less humble?
Can you spend one difficult moment today as the field's witness rather than its owner?

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
प्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव क्षेत्रं क्षेत्रज्ञमेव च ।
एतद्वेदितुमिच्छामि ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं च केशव॥
verses.transliteration:
prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva kṣetraṃ kṣetrajñameva ca
etadveditumicchāmi jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ ca keśava
verses.essence: Arjuna asks: prakriti and purusha, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and the object of knowledge — these I wish to understand, Keshava.
verses.translation: I wish to learn about Nature (matter) and the Spirit (soul), the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and that which ought to be known, O Kesava.

anvaya.parts: क्षेत्र (field) + ज्ञ (knower) — one who knows the field

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), neuter, accusative singular (object)

anvaya.base: केशव · Keshava, a name of Krishna

verses.explanation: Six technical terms in one breath: Arjuna requests the conceptual machinery beneath everything he has heard — matter and spirit, the field and its witness, knowing and the known. The Gita's final movement begins here: after love's chapters, the anatomy lesson; after the vision, the vocabulary to hold it.
verses.connection: Opens Part Three of the Gita: the analytic chapters that give bhakti its metaphysical skeleton.
verses.reflection: Ask for the map beneath your experience today: what is the field here, and who is knowing it?
verses.background: Chapter 13 opens with a new request from Arjuna. Some editions leave this verse out and start the chapter with Krishna's reply. Arjuna lists the pairs of terms he wants explained: nature and spirit, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and what is to be known.
verses.text_note: This verse (Arjuna’s question) is absent from the critical edition and from Śaṅkara’s and Rāmānuja’s text; editions that omit it count 700 verses and number the rest of chapter 13 one lower.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna want to understand at the start of this teaching?

views.text: Notes that many editions omit this verse (with it the Gita has 701). Reads it as opening the third section: the same teaching in more detail, answering what knowledge the devotee dear to the Lord in chapter 12 should have.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
इदं शरीरं कौन्तेय क्षेत्रमित्यभिधीयते ।
एतद्यो वेत्ति तं प्राहुः क्षेत्रज्ञ इति तद्विदः॥
verses.transliteration:
idaṃ śarīraṃ kaunteya kṣetramityabhidhīyate
etadyo vetti taṃ prāhuḥ kṣetrajña iti tadvidaḥ
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: this body, Kaunteya, is called the field; the one who knows it — him the knowers of truth call the knower of the field.
verses.translation: This body, O Arjuna, is called the field; he who knows it is called the knower of the field, by those who know of them.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, nominative singular (what it is called)

anvaya.base: thus; marks a quotation or name

anvaya.form: verb, perfect used as present, 3rd person plural
noun, masculine, nominative singular (the name quoted by इति)
anvaya.parts: क्षेत्र (field) + ज्ञ (knower) — one who knows the field

anvaya.base: thus; marks a quotation or name

anvaya.parts: तद् (that) + विद् (knower) — those who know that truth

verses.explanation: The founding distinction, drawn in a farmer's metaphor: kṣetra, the field — this body, where the harvest of past actions comes up as pleasure and pain — and kṣetrajña, the one who *knows* it. The move is small and seismic: whatever you can observe about yourself, from head to foot, you are not it; you are the observing. A field is sown and reaped, and what is planted in this one across a life will come up. The knower watches; the field grows. The rest of the chapter unpacks these two words.
verses.connection: The chapter's axiom: everything else (13.3–35) is commentary on this one cut.
verses.reflection: Run the founding experiment once: whatever you can observe in yourself, note — observed, therefore not me.
verses.background: Arjuna has just asked to learn about nature and spirit, the field and its knower, knowledge and what is to be known. Krishna begins his answer. Śrīdhara gives the reason: Krishna promised in chapter 12 to lift his devotees out of the sea of death and rebirth, and that rescue needs knowledge of the self.
verses.hook: What is meant by the field, and who is its knower?

views.text: Derives kṣetra three ways: protected from decay, perishing, or the place where the fruits of action ripen. The knower is whoever makes the whole body, head to foot, an object of knowledge distinct from himself.

Everyday talk like 'I am a man, I am fat' identifies self and body, yet we also say 'I know this body'. What is known as an object must differ from its knower, a self seen only by a mind refined in yoga.
Opens the chapter as the fulfilment of the promise to lift devotees out of saṃsāra, which needs self-knowledge. The body is called the field because it is the ground where saṃsāra sprouts.
The field is not the physical body alone: physical, mental and causal bodies together make it up, and in it the harvest of actions is reaped as pleasure and pain.

The soul cannot act alone and works through the body, mind and intellect, its field of activity; because it knows this field it is called its knower, though in forgetfulness it identifies with the field.

verses.devanagari:
क्षेत्रज्ञं चापि मां विद्धि सर्वक्षेत्रेषु भारत ।
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञयोर्ज्ञानं यत्तज्ज्ञानं मतं मम॥
verses.transliteration:
kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi māṃ viddhi sarvakṣetreṣu bhārata
kṣetrakṣetrajñayorjñānaṃ yattajjñānaṃ mataṃ mama
verses.essence: And know me also as the knower of the field in all fields, Bharata. The knowledge of field and field-knower — that, in my view, is true knowledge.
verses.translation: Do thou also know Me as the knower of the field in all fields, O Arjuna. Knowledge of both the field and the knower of the field is considered by Me to be the knowledge.

anvaya.parts: क्षेत्र (field) + ज्ञ (knower) — one who knows the field
सर्व (all) + क्षेत्र (field) — in all the fields

anvaya.meaning: of the field and its knower
anvaya.base: क्षेत्र · field; क्षेत्रज्ञ · knower of the field
anvaya.form: noun, masculine, genitive dual (of the two)
anvaya.parts: क्षेत्र (field) + क्षेत्रज्ञ (field-knower) — the pair, field and field-knower

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular (held, considered)

verses.explanation: The verse that detonates the tidy dualism a breath after it was drawn: the knower in *all* fields is — me. Behind every pair of eyes, the one who is speaking claims to be the knower — in Arjuna, in Krishna, in the soldier across the battlefield. And the definition narrows: of all that can be learned, only *this* — field and knower told apart — earns the name knowledge. The schools divide over the first line: for Shankara one Witness, its many forms only the play of limiting adjuncts; for Ramanuja many real souls, all ensouled by one inner Lord. Either way, the private knower of 13.2 has just been opened onto God.
verses.connection: Raises 13.2's psychology into theology: the private witness identified as the universal one.
verses.reflection: Greet the knower behind one other pair of eyes today as the same knower behind yours.
verses.background: Krishna has just called the body the field and the one who knows it the knower of the field. Śaṅkara asks whether that much is enough to understand them, and answers no: Krishna now says who that knower really is, and what he himself counts as knowledge.
verses.hook: Who knows every field, and what counts as true knowledge?

views.text: The knower in every field, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, is the one God, appearing many only through limiting adjuncts. Difference between knowledge and ignorance answers the objection that God would then suffer saṃsāra.
Field and field-knowers are the Lord's body and cannot exist apart from him, so they can be called one with him, as the inner Controller of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka passage dwells in and rules every self.

For worldly people the soul, covered in dirt, is the field-knower; for the enlightened it is Vāsudeva, the one by whose grace the insentient body becomes sentient. 'Knows' carries a causative sense here: he makes the field know.
The bound jīva, in truth, is the Lord himself, as 'tat tvam asi' teaches. Only the knowledge that tells field from knower frees; all other learning is mere cleverness that binds.
The soul knows only its own body, and imperfectly; God, the Supreme Soul in every heart, knows all fields fully. True knowledge is knowing the body, the soul and God, and how they differ.

verses.devanagari:
तत्क्षेत्रं यच्च यादृक्च यद्विकारि यतश्च यत् ।
स च यो यत्प्रभावश्च तत्समासेन मे शृणु॥
verses.transliteration:
tatkṣetraṃ yacca yādṛkca yadvikāri yataśca yat
sa ca yo yatprabhāvaśca tatsamāsena me śṛṇu
verses.essence: What that field is, of what kind, what its modifications, whence it arises and what it is; and who he is and what his powers — hear that from me in brief.
verses.translation: What the field is and of what nature, what are its modifications and whence it is and also who He is and what His powers are hear all that from Me in brief.

anvaya.parts: यद् (which) + विकारिन् (having changes) — having which modifications
यद् (which) + प्रभाव (power) — one whose powers are which

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by way of)
pronoun, short form of genitive singular, here 'from me'

verses.explanation: The syllabus: five questions about the field, two about its knower — a complete research program announced in two lines. Samāsena, in brief: the Gita is about to compress all of Sankhya's category-science into a handful of verses, then point beyond what Sankhya ever mapped.
verses.connection: Table of contents for 13.6–19: the field analyzed, then the knower's true nature.
verses.reflection: Approach yourself like a researcher today: what is this field, whence, with what changes, and whose?
verses.background: With field and knower named and the knowledge of both praised, Krishna lays out what he will go on to explain. Śaṅkara calls this a brief statement of the subject, given first because a teaching should be introduced before it is expanded. Krishna promises only a summary.
verses.hook: What will Krishna explain about the field and its knower?

views.text: The Lord promises a brief account of the field, this body, with its qualities, changes and causes, and of the Knower of the field and his powers, powers that arise from the adjuncts.

Takes the questions as the field's substance, what depends on it, its transformations, the purpose for which it arose, and its true nature; 'he' is the individual self, with its own nature and powers.
The field is inert and seen; 'whence' means it arises from the union of prakṛti and puruṣa. The knower's powers come from inconceivable lordship.
Builds an allegory: the body is the field, the ten senses its bulls, the mind the overseer, the soul the tenant, the vital airs the labourers, and Nature the mistress who owns it.

verses.devanagari:
ऋषिभिर्बहुधा गीतं छन्दोभिर्विविधैः पृथक् ।
ब्रह्मसूत्रपदैश्चैव हेतुमद्भिर्विनिश्चितैः॥
verses.transliteration:
ṛṣibhirbahudhā gītaṃ chandobhirvividhaiḥ pṛthak
brahmasūtrapadaiścaiva hetumadbhirviniścitaiḥ
verses.essence: It has been sung by the seers in many ways, in various hymns distinctly — and in the words of the Brahma-sutras, reasoned and conclusive.
verses.translation: Sages have sung in many ways, in various distinctive chants and also in the suggestive words indicative of the Absolute, full of reasoning and decisive.

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular (sung)

anvaya.meaning: by words of the aphorisms on Brahman
anvaya.parts: ब्रह्म (Brahman) + सूत्र (aphorism) + पद (word) — words that point to Brahman

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, instrumental plural

verses.explanation: A bibliography, and a humility rare in revelation: this teaching is not novel — the seers sang it, the hymns scattered it, and the sutra-style aphorisms argued it with hetumat, *reasons*. The Gita places itself inside a tradition of both poetry and logic, claiming to distill rather than invent.
verses.connection: Credentials the analysis to come: ancient, plural, and argued — not asserted.
verses.reflection: Lean on the lineage when your own seeing tires — seers sang this, sutras argued it, before you.
verses.background: Krishna has promised to explain the field and its knower in brief. Śrīdhara frames the question this invites: a summary of what, and who told it at length? Krishna answers by pointing to the seers and the scriptures that taught it before him.
verses.hook: Where has this knowledge of the field been taught before?

refs.note: The Vedas came forth as the breath of God; this grounds the claim that the seers' Vedic teaching is a reliable authority.
Every spiritual principle is established on the authority of the Vedas.

views.text: Brahma-sūtra-padas are the Upanishadic sentences that indicate Brahman and through which it is reached, such as 'the Self alone is to be meditated upon'; 'decisive' means they give certain, not ambiguous, knowledge.

Cites Parāśara's Viṣṇu Purāṇa and the Taittirīya's layered selves to show the seers taught body, individual self, and the Supreme Self within both, with Vāsudeva as the Self of field and knower alike.

Splits the compound: sūtras are Upanishadic passages marking Brahman by its relation to the world ('from which beings are born'); padas are those defining its own nature ('truth, knowledge, infinite').
Takes the phrase as Bādarāyaṇa's Brahma Sūtras, also called the Śārīraka Sūtras because a group of them treats the body, the field.
Spiritual knowledge must be clear, logical and confirmed by a reliable authority, and that authority is the Vedas, God's eternal knowledge, together with the scriptures that conform to them.

verses.devanagari:
महाभूतान्यहंकारो बुद्धिरव्यक्तमेव च ।
इन्द्रियाणि दशैकं च पञ्च चेन्द्रियगोचराः॥
verses.transliteration:
mahābhūtānyahaṃkāro buddhiravyaktameva ca
indriyāṇi daśaikaṃ ca pañca cendriyagocarāḥ
verses.essence: The great elements, the ego, the understanding, and the unmanifest; the ten senses and the one mind, and the five pastures of the senses —
verses.translation: The great elements, egoism, intellect, and also the Unmanifested Nature, the ten senses and one (mind), and the five objects of the senses.

anvaya.parts: महत् (great) + भूत (element) — the great elements
अहम् (I) + कार (maker) — that which makes 'I'

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + गोचर (range, pasture) — the ranges where the senses roam

verses.explanation: The field surveyed with Sankhya's instruments: all twenty-four categories in a single verse. Earth to ether, the I-maker, the intellect, the unmanifest seed-state of matter; ten senses of knowing and doing, the mind that coordinates them, and the five 'pastures' — go-cara, where the sense-cattle graze. Everything objectifiable is going on this list.
verses.connection: Begins the field-inventory of 13.4's first question — completed by 13.7.
verses.reflection: Inventory your equipment without flinching today: elements, senses, mind, ego — all of it, field.
verses.background: Arjuna's interest roused, Krishna starts on the first point he promised: what the field is. Śrīdhara notes that the answer takes two verses. This first one gives the components that the Sāṃkhya (analytic) school counts as twenty-four principles, from the great elements and the unmanifest down to the senses and their objects.
verses.hook: What elements make up the field of the body?

views.text: The 'great elements' here are the subtle ones; the gross elements are the sense-objects. The unmanifest is God's power, the māyā of 7.14; with the rest these make Sankhya's twenty-four categories.
Divides the list: elements, ahaṅkāra (here the primal element), mahat and prakṛti are the substances that produce the field; the eleven senses and five objects are principles that depend on it.
All of these, elements, ego, intellect, senses and mind, are reabsorbed into the Unmanifest at cosmic dissolution; the mind itself is counted as māyā.

The field consists of twenty-four elements: the five gross elements, five sense objects, ten senses, mind, intellect, ego and primordial matter; the same body can also be seen as five sheaths covering the soul.

verses.devanagari:
इच्छा द्वेषः सुखं दुःखं संघातश्चेतना धृतिः ।
एतत्क्षेत्रं समासेन सविकारमुदाहृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
icchā dveṣaḥ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ saṃghātaścetanā dhṛtiḥ
etatkṣetraṃ samāsena savikāramudāhṛtam
verses.essence: — desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the bodily aggregate, awareness, steadfastness: this is the field, briefly described with its modifications.
verses.translation: Desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, the aggregate (the body), intelligence, fortitude the field has thus been briefly described with its modifications.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by way of)

anvaya.parts: स (with) + विकार (modification) — together with its modifications

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The inventory's quiet shock: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain — even cetanā, the light of awareness as a *function* — all filed under field, not knower. What you want, what you flee, what you feel, even your moods of clarity: observable, therefore not you. The self just lost everything it usually calls itself, and kept only the seeing.
verses.connection: Completes the field-list — and relocates the entire inner life to the 'known' side of 13.2's line.
verses.reflection: File one strong feeling correctly today: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain — contents of the field, not the seer.
verses.background: With the twenty-four principles listed, this second verse adds the inner states, and Śaṅkara says why: even qualities that the Vaiśeṣika school counts as attributes of the soul, such as desire and pleasure, belong to the field and not to its knower. The verse closes the description of the field.
verses.hook: What changes and states belong to the field?

views.text: Each item counts as field because it is an object of knowledge. Sentience is a state of the internal organ lit by a semblance of the Self's consciousness, like fire glowing in a heated lump of iron.

Desire, hatred, pleasure and pain are modifications of the field, though they arise in the self through its contact with the field. Reads the aggregate as the support of the conscious self, its base for experience and for release.
Takes dhṛti as the feeling 'this much is enough for me' that arises in every being, from Brahmā down to a worm, at the close of an action, a consolation that keeps life going.
The field includes the body with its six changes, the consciousness the soul lends it, will, desire, aversion, pleasure and pain; desires for the world bind, while desire for God frees.

verses.devanagari:
अमानित्वमदम्भित्वमहिंसा क्षान्तिरार्जवम् ।
आचार्योपासनं शौचं स्थैर्यमात्मविनिग्रहः॥
verses.transliteration:
amānitvamadambhitvamahiṃsā kṣāntirārjavam
ācāryopāsanaṃ śaucaṃ sthairyamātmavinigrahaḥ
verses.essence: Humility, unpretentiousness, harmlessness, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-restraint —
verses.translation: Humility, unpretentiousness, non-injury, forgiveness, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-control.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + मानिन् (proud) + त्व (-ness) — not being proud
अ (not) + दम्भिन् (pretender) + त्व (-ness) — not making a show
अ (not) + हिंसा (harming) — not harming
आचार्य (teacher) + उपासन (attendance) — attending on the teacher
आत्मन् (self, body-mind) + विनिग्रह (restraint) — restraint of oneself

verses.explanation: Now the fifth term of 13.1 — *knowledge* — and the definition startles: not propositions but properties. The list opens with amānitvam, the deflating of self-importance, and adambhitvam, the end of performance. Knowledge, in this chapter, is not what a person holds; it is what a person has become.
verses.connection: Begins the famous twenty marks of knowledge (13.8–12): epistemology as character.
verses.reflection: Practice the first marks today: one act of unpretentious humility, one harm consciously not done.
verses.background: The field has been described. Before describing its knower, Krishna gives the means to know him, and Śrīdhara notes this takes five verses. This first verse begins the list with qualities of conduct, called knowledge because they lead to it and make a seeker fit for it.
verses.hook: What qualities must you grow to gain true knowledge?

refs.note: Purity is of two kinds, outer and inner; it supports the cleanliness of body and mind named among the marks of knowledge.

views.text: Purity is both outer, washing the body, and inner, removing attachment and the like by thinking of their opposites; self-control means keeping the body-mind aggregate, which strays everywhere, to the right path.

Reads several marks pointedly: humility is no superiority toward the eminent; unpretentiousness is not practising dharma for fame; steadiness is unshakable faith in the scriptures on the self; self-control is turning away from all that is not the self.
These are marks by which wisdom can be inferred: where they appear complete, self-knowledge has dawned. Separates pride, which has something to boast of, from vanity, which boasts of nothing.

These verses list the habits and attitudes that purify the heart, since knowledge of the field and its knower is not bookish learning but needs a changed character: humility, honesty, non-violence, forgiveness, service of the Guru, purity and steadiness.

verses.devanagari:
इन्द्रियार्थेषु वैराग्यमनहंकार एव च ।
जन्ममृत्युजराव्याधिदुःखदोषानुदर्शनम्॥
verses.transliteration:
indriyārtheṣu vairāgyamanahaṃkāra eva ca
janmamṛtyujarāvyādhiduḥkhadoṣānudarśanam
verses.essence: — dispassion toward the objects of sense, absence of ego, and keeping in sight the suffering and fault in birth, death, old age and disease —
verses.translation: Indifference to the objects of the senses and also absence of egoism; perception of (or reflection on) the evil in birth, death, old age, sickness and pain.

anvaya.meaning: toward the objects of the senses
anvaya.parts: इन्द्रिय (sense) + अर्थ (object) — the objects of the senses
अन् (not) + अहङ्कार (ego) — being without ego

anvaya.meaning: seeing the evils of birth, death, age, sickness
anvaya.parts: जन्म (birth) + मृत्यु (death) + जरा (old age) + व्याधि (disease) + दुःख (pain) + दोष (fault) + अनुदर्शन (repeated seeing) — keeping in view the pain and fault in birth, death, old age and disease

verses.explanation: Anudarśanam — *keeping in view*: the knower does not morbidly dwell on mortality but declines to look away from it. Birth, death, age, disease held steadily in the visual field, the way a navigator holds the reef. Most delusion is maintained by selective attention; knowledge begins as the refusal to curate.
verses.connection: The marks continue inward: clear-eyed about the body's full itinerary.
verses.reflection: Keep mortality in peripheral vision today — not morbidly, just unfiltered — and watch priorities sort.
verses.background: The list of qualities that lead to knowledge continues into its second verse. After the outward conduct of the first, it turns inward: to the seeker's stance toward the objects of the senses, toward his own ego, and toward what every embodied life must pass through.
verses.hook: What attitude toward the senses and life's pains belongs to knowledge?

refs.note: Purity is of two kinds, outer and inner; it supports the cleanliness of body and mind named among the marks of knowledge.

views.text: Birth and the rest are miseries because they cause misery. Reflecting on this breeds dispassion for body and objects, turns the senses toward the inner Self, and so is called knowledge as a cause of knowledge.
Absence of egoism means freedom from taking the body for the self, and by extension from claiming as one's own what does not belong to one.
Anudarśana means reviewing again and again; the compound can also be read as seeing the fault that is itself pain.

These verses list the habits and attitudes that purify the heart, since knowledge of the field and its knower is not bookish learning but needs a changed character: humility, honesty, non-violence, forgiveness, service of the Guru, purity and steadiness.

verses.devanagari:
असक्तिरनभिष्वङ्गः पुत्रदारगृहादिषु ।
नित्यं च समचित्तत्वमिष्टानिष्टोपपत्तिषु॥
verses.transliteration:
asaktiranabhiṣvaṅgaḥ putradāragṛhādiṣu
nityaṃ ca samacittatvamiṣṭāniṣṭopapattiṣu
verses.essence: — non-attachment, absence of clinging to son, wife and home; constant even-mindedness amid wished-for and unwished-for events —
verses.translation: Non-attachment, non-identification of the Self with son, wife, home and the rest, and constant even-mindedness on the attainment of the desirable and the undesirable.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + सक्ति (attachment) — not clinging
अन् (not) + अभिष्वङ्ग (intense clinging) — not being entangled

anvaya.meaning: toward son, wife, home and the rest
anvaya.parts: पुत्र (son) + दार (wife) + गृह (home) + आदि (and the rest) — son, wife, home and so on
सम (even) + चित्त (mind) + त्व (-ness) — having an even mind

anvaya.meaning: when the wanted and unwanted arrive
anvaya.parts: इष्ट (desired) + अनिष्ट (undesired) + उपपत्ति (arrival) — the coming of the desired and undesired

verses.explanation: The list walks into the house: putra-dāra-gṛha — son, spouse, home. Not their abandonment — the word is anabhiṣvaṅga, the absence of *entanglement*, love without the white-knuckle grip that mistakes possession for devotion. The hardest mark on the list, because it must be practiced at the breakfast table.
verses.connection: The marks reach the domestic — where detachment is most easily preached and least easily lived.
verses.reflection: Love your nearest without the clutch for one evening — entanglement loosened, affection intact.
verses.background: Third of the five verses on the means to knowledge. Having dealt with dispassion toward sense-objects and the ego, the list moves to the seeker's ties with family and household, and to how his mind meets fortune both wanted and unwanted.
verses.hook: How should a seeker hold family, home and life's ups and downs?

refs.note: Purity is of two kinds, outer and inner; it supports the cleanliness of body and mind named among the marks of knowledge.

views.text: Abhiṣvaṅga is a special attachment of self-identification: feeling 'I am happy' or 'I shall die' when a son or wife is happy or dies. Its absence, extended even to dear servants, is called knowledge.
Not abandoning family but freedom from affection for son, wife and home beyond the limits the scriptures allow.
The wise treat their home like a public inn beside the road: they stay there without the clinging that makes another's death one's own grief.

These verses list the habits and attitudes that purify the heart, since knowledge of the field and its knower is not bookish learning but needs a changed character: humility, honesty, non-violence, forgiveness, service of the Guru, purity and steadiness.

verses.devanagari:
मयि चानन्ययोगेन भक्तिरव्यभिचारिणी ।
विविक्तदेशसेवित्वमरतिर्जनसंसदि॥
verses.transliteration:
mayi cānanyayogena bhaktiravyabhicāriṇī
viviktadeśasevitvamaratirjanasaṃsadi
verses.essence: — unswerving devotion to me with undivided yoga, resort to solitary places, distaste for crowds of people —
verses.translation: Unswerving devotion unto Me by the Yoga of non-separation, resort to solitary places, distaste for the society of men.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: अनन्य (no other) + योग (yoga) — a yoga with no other object
अ (not) + व्यभिचारिन् (straying) — never straying
विविक्त (secluded, pure) + देश (place) + सेवित्व (habit of resorting) — the habit of frequenting secluded places
अ (not) + रति (delight) — taking no pleasure
जन (people) + संसद् (assembly) — a gathering of people

verses.explanation: In the middle of an austere Sankhya catalogue, suddenly: bhakti — unswerving, undivided, addressed to *me*. The placement is the teaching: even in the Gita's most analytic chapter, devotion is listed as a component of knowledge itself, not its rival. Solitude and crowd-weariness follow as its natural climate.
verses.connection: Devotion planted at the heart of the knowledge-list — chapter 12 echoing inside chapter 13.
verses.reflection: Give devotion its place in your knowledge today — and take ten minutes of genuine solitude.
verses.background: Fourth of the five verses listing the means to knowledge. Here the list turns to the seeker's relation to Krishna himself and to the company and surroundings he chooses. Śaṅkara counts these too as knowledge, because they lead to it.
verses.hook: What do devotion and solitude have to do with knowledge?

refs.note: Purity is of two kinds, outer and inner; it supports the cleanliness of body and mind named among the marks of knowledge.

views.text: Ananya-yoga is the settled conviction that none is higher than Vāsudeva, he alone the goal. The distaste is for crowds of uncultured people, not for gatherings of the pure, which help knowledge.
The 'yoga of non-difference' is the conviction that nothing exists apart from the Lord; such devotion cannot fail, because the desires that cause failure are either absent or absorbed in him.
Pictures the devotee merged in God as a river in the ocean; solitude calms the mind for meditation, while company of the wise, satsaṅga, still helps.

These verses list the habits and attitudes that purify the heart, since knowledge of the field and its knower is not bookish learning but needs a changed character: humility, honesty, non-violence, forgiveness, service of the Guru, purity and steadiness.

verses.devanagari:
अध्यात्मज्ञाननित्यत्वं तत्त्वज्ञानार्थदर्शनम् ।
एतज्ज्ञानमिति प्रोक्तमज्ञानं यदतोऽन्यथा॥
verses.transliteration:
adhyātmajñānanityatvaṃ tattvajñānārthadarśanam
etajjñānamiti proktamajñānaṃ yadato'nyathā
verses.essence: — constancy in the knowledge of the inner self, insight into the purpose of knowing the truth: this is declared to be knowledge. Ignorance is what is otherwise.
verses.translation: Constancy in Self-knowledge, perception of the end of true knowledge this is declared to be knowledge, and what is opposed to it is ignorance.

anvaya.meaning: constancy in knowledge of the self
anvaya.parts: अध्यात्म (concerning the self) + ज्ञान (knowledge) + नित्यत्व (constancy) — abiding always in self-knowledge

anvaya.meaning: keeping in view the goal of truth-knowledge
anvaya.parts: तत्त्व (truth) + ज्ञान (knowledge) + अर्थ (aim) + दर्शन (seeing) — seeing the aim of knowing the truth

anvaya.base: thus; marks a quotation or name

anvaya.form: past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The twenty marks close, and the definition is sealed both ways: etat jñānam — *this* is knowledge, this lived constellation of humility, clarity, evenness, love — and everything else, however erudite, ajñānam. A person could hold every text and miss the list; a person could hold the list and need no text. The chapter has redefined learning as transformation.
verses.connection: Seals 13.8–12 and clears the stage for the last term of 13.1: the thing to be known.
verses.reflection: Measure your learning tonight by the list, not the library: has knowing become character?
verses.background: The last of the five verses on the means to knowledge. It adds two final items about where the seeker's mind dwells, then names the whole list, which Śrīdhara counts as twenty qualities, and sets it against its opposite.
verses.hook: What is true knowledge, and what is ignorance?

refs.note: Purity is of two kinds, outer and inner; it supports the cleanliness of body and mind named among the marks of knowledge.

views.text: The goal of knowing the truth is liberation; contemplating it rouses one to the disciplines. The twenty marks are called knowledge because they lead to it; their opposites, arrogance, cruelty and the like, are ignorance to be avoided.
Constancy in self-knowledge means being fixed in the purified sense of 'thou' (tvam-pada); seeing the goal means reflecting on the supremacy of liberation. Counts the marks as twenty.
Cultivate the virtues and the opposite traits die off by themselves, like garden plants left without water; fighting the vices head-on is hard.

These verses list the habits and attitudes that purify the heart, since knowledge of the field and its knower is not bookish learning but needs a changed character: humility, honesty, non-violence, forgiveness, service of the Guru, purity and steadiness.

verses.devanagari:
ज्ञेयं यत्तत्प्रवक्ष्यामि यज्ज्ञात्वामृतमश्नुते ।
अनादिमत्परं ब्रह्म न सत्तन्नासदुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
jñeyaṃ yattatpravakṣyāmi yajjñātvāmṛtamaśnute
anādi matparaṃ brahma na sattannāsaducyate
verses.essence: I shall declare that which is to be known, knowing which one attains immortality: the beginningless supreme Brahman, said to be neither being nor non-being.
verses.translation: I will declare that which has to be known, knowing which one attains to immortality, the beginningless supreme Brahman, called neither being nor non-being.

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: अनादि (without beginning) + -मत् (having) — that which has no beginning (Rāmānuja instead splits अनादि + मत्परम्, 'having Me as highest')

anvaya.form: present participle used as noun, neuter, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The jñeya, the knowable, introduced with the highest stakes — amṛtam aśnute, one *attains* deathlessness — and immediately placed beyond the mind's most basic sorting: na sat tan nāsad ucyate, neither 'is' nor 'is not.' Not because it is vague, but because is/is-not are categories of the field, and this is what the field appears *in*.
verses.connection: Opens the Brahman-hymn (13.13–18): the knowable that breaks the knower's grammar.
verses.reflection: Sit one minute with what is neither 'is' nor 'is not' — the knowable that breaks the sorting.
verses.background: The means to knowledge have been listed; Krishna now turns to what that knowledge is of. Śrīdhara notes that this description of the thing to be known runs six verses. Krishna opens it by stating the reward of knowing it, to win the listener's attention.
verses.hook: What is the one thing worth knowing that leads to immortality?

views.text: Reads anādimat as one word, the extra -mat filling the metre, and rejects the split 'matparam' because the verse aims to make Brahman known only by negating every attribute, as 'not this, not this' does.
The 'brahman' to be known here is the individual self: beginningless, having the Lord as its highest, and taking on its infinite nature once freed from karma.

'Being' names what positive means of knowledge reach and 'non-being' what negation reaches; Brahman is unlike both because it is no object. Allows the split 'matparam' too: my, Viṣṇu's, supreme attributeless form.
9.19 called him both being and non-being; here he is neither. Both statements hold: the manifest and unmanifest are his forms, and he is beyond both.

Brahman lies beyond the paired terms of being and non-being; the formless Brahman, the Supreme Soul within and the personal Lord are three aspects of one Reality, and Krishna now describes its paradoxical qualities.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वतः पाणिपादं तत्सर्वतोऽक्षिशिरोमुखम् ।
सर्वतः श्रुतिमल्लोके सर्वमावृत्य तिष्ठति॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvataḥ pāṇipādaṃ tatsarvato'kṣiśiromukham
sarvataḥ śrutimalloke sarvamāvṛtya tiṣṭhati
verses.essence: With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and mouths everywhere, with hearing everywhere — That stands in the world, enveloping all.
verses.translation: With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and mouths everywhere, with ears everywhere, He exists in the worlds enveloping all.

anvaya.parts: पाणि (hand) + पाद (foot) — that which has hands and feet

anvaya.base: अक्षि · eye; शिरस् · head; मुख · mouth, face
anvaya.parts: अक्षि (eye) + शिरस् (head) + मुख (mouth, face) — that which has eyes, heads and faces

verses.explanation: The Upanishadic image (Shvetashvatara's verse, quoted whole): every hand in the world is its hand, every eye its eye. Read it backward and it becomes practice: whatever hand you take, whatever face you meet, you are touching the jñeya. The all-faced form of chapter 11 returns — as everyday perception rather than overwhelming vision.
verses.connection: The knowable located: not elsewhere, but as the everywhere — ch11's vision in still life.
verses.reflection: See one hand at work today — anyone's — as His hand; one face as His face everywhere.
verses.background: Krishna has just said the thing to be known is neither being nor non-being. Śaṅkara points to the worry this raises, that it may not exist at all; to dispel it, Krishna shows its presence through the organs of every living creature.
verses.hook: Does the Supreme have hands, eyes and ears, and where?

refs.note: All this is Brahman; since God is everywhere, his eyes and ears are everywhere too.

views.text: Hands, feet and eyes belong to the adjuncts, the bodies; they are attributed to the Knowable only to show that it exists, then denied, following the rule that the Transcendent is taught by superimposition and its retraction.
Reads 'That' as the pure individual self, which, freed and all-pervasive, can do the work of hands, feet and eyes everywhere, sharing equality with the Lord.
Answers the worry that 'neither being nor non-being' means a void: the Knowable drives body and senses as an engine-driver drives an engine, the inner Ruler of all.
We should not limit God: he has hands, eyes and ears without number, divine rather than material and present everywhere, so he sees all, hears every prayer and accepts offerings made anywhere.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वेन्द्रियगुणाभासं सर्वेन्द्रियविवर्जितम् ।
असक्तं सर्वभृच्चैव निर्गुणं गुणभोक्तृ च॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvendriyaguṇābhāsaṃ sarvendriyavivarjitam
asaktaṃ sarvabhṛccaiva nirguṇaṃ guṇabhoktṛ ca
verses.essence: Shining through all the senses' qualities, yet free of all senses; unattached, yet the sustainer of all; without gunas, yet the experiencer of gunas —
verses.translation: Shining by the functions of all the senses, yet without the senses; unattached, yet supporting all; devoid of qualities, yet their experiencer.

anvaya.meaning: shining through the functions of all senses
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + इन्द्रिय (sense) + गुण (function) + आभास (shining) — appearing through the workings of all the senses
सर्व (all) + इन्द्रिय (sense) + विवर्जित (free of) — without any of the senses
अ (not) + सक्त (attached) — unattached
सर्व (all) + भृत् (bearer) — that which bears all
निस् (without) + गुण (guna) — without the three gunas

anvaya.form: noun used as adjective, neuter, nominative singular
anvaya.parts: गुण (guna) + भोक्तृ (experiencer) — the one who experiences the gunas

verses.explanation: Three paradoxes in two lines, each the same shape: present in X, free of X. It lights up every sense without owning one; carries everything while holding nothing; tastes the gunas' whole play from outside their reach. Contradiction is the only honest syntax for what stands on both sides of every distinction.
verses.connection: The hymn's method declared: the knowable describable only in paired opposites.
verses.reflection: Practice a paradox today: be fully present in your senses, and quietly free of them.
verses.background: Krishna has just pictured the knowable with hands, feet, eyes and ears everywhere. Śaṅkara says this verse follows so that no one takes those organs as truly its own: they belong to the beings it pervades, and the knowable stands apart from them.
verses.hook: How can the Supreme be without senses, yet perceive through them all?

refs.note: Without hands or feet he grasps and moves; without eyes or ears he sees and hears, the same pairing of opposites as this verse.
The Supreme Lord holds within himself countless contradictory attributes.

views.text: It seems active through the organs' functions, as 'it thinks, as it were' (Bṛh. 4.3.7) says, yet has no instruments. It supports all because existence underlies everything; even a mirage needs a ground.
The self can know objects through the senses, yet can also know everything by itself; by nature it is unattached to divine or human bodies, yet able to support them.
Takes guṇa-bhoktṛ as both experiencer and protector of the gunas, and cites the Śvetāśvatara: 'without hands or feet he moves and grasps, sees without eyes, hears without ears'.

God holds opposite qualities at once beyond ordinary logic: without material senses, yet with divine senses everywhere; sustainer of all, yet detached and complete in himself; enjoyer of the gunas, yet beyond them.

verses.devanagari:
बहिरन्तश्च भूतानामचरं चरमेव च ।
सूक्ष्मत्वात्तदविज्ञेयं दूरस्थं चान्तिके च तत्॥
verses.transliteration:
bahirantaśca bhūtānāmacaraṃ carameva ca
sūkṣmatvāttadavijñeyaṃ dūrasthaṃ cāntike ca tat
verses.essence: Outside all beings and within them; unmoving and yet moving; too subtle to be known; far away, and also near —
verses.translation: Without and within (all) beings the unmoving and also the moving; because of Its subtlety, unknowable; and near and far away is That.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + चर (moving) — not moving
सूक्ष्म (subtle) + त्व (-ness) — subtlety

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), negated, neuter, nominative singular
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + विज्ञेय (knowable) — not knowable
दूर (far) + स्थ (standing) — situated far off

verses.explanation: The paradoxes turn spatial: outside and inside, far and near — dūra-stham cāntike ca, echoing the Isha Upanishad. 'Far' for the mind that seeks it as an object across some distance; 'near' — nearer than near — for the one who notices it was never absent from a single moment of seeking. The distance was the looking.
verses.connection: Continues 13.15's paradox-chain into geography: the knowable has no 'where.'
verses.reflection: Find the far-and-near once today: sought as an object, distant; noticed as the noticing, here.
verses.background: The description of the knowable continues. Having set its working through the senses beside its freedom from them, Krishna now places it in relation to beings themselves, to motion and stillness, and to distance, and gives the reason it is so hard to know.
verses.hook: Is the Supreme far away or near, inside us or outside?

refs.note: It moves and does not move, is far and near, within all and outside all, almost the same words as this verse.

views.text: Even the moving and unmoving body is the Knowable, as a rope appears as a snake. It is far for the ignorant, unreachable in millions of years, and near as the very Self of the enlightened.
The self can exist outside the body and within it; unmoving by nature, it moves when embodied. It is far from those who lack modesty and the other virtues, and near to those who have them.
It is within and without beings as gold is in its bracelets and water in its waves; cites the Īśa mantra 'it moves and moves not, it is far and it is near'.
God is said to be both knowable and unknowable: he cannot be grasped by the senses, mind or intellect, which are material, but those he graces come to know him.

verses.devanagari:
अविभक्तं च भूतेषु विभक्तमिव च स्थितम् ।
भूतभर्तृ च तज्ज्ञेयं ग्रसिष्णु प्रभविष्णु च॥
verses.transliteration:
avibhaktaṃ ca bhūteṣu vibhaktamiva ca sthitam
bhūtabhartṛ ca tajjñeyaṃ grasiṣṇu prabhaviṣṇu ca
verses.essence: Undivided, yet standing as if divided among beings; That, the knowable, is the sustainer of beings — their devourer, and their generator.
verses.translation: And undivided, yet It exists as if divided in beings; It is to be known as the supporter of being; It devours and It generates.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + विभक्त (divided): 'not divided'
भूत (beings) + भर्तृ (supporter): 'the supporter of beings'

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), neuter, nominative singular
adjective in -iṣṇu (tending to devour), neuter, nominative singular
adjective in -iṣṇu (tending to originate), neuter, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The crucial iva — *as if* divided: one light through many windows looks like many lights; the partition belongs to the windows. Then the full job description in three titles: bhūta-bhartṛ, sustainer of beings; grasiṣṇu, their devourer; prabhaviṣṇu, their generator — the mouths of chapter 11 and the seed of chapter 7, the same one knowable wearing all three offices.
verses.connection: Resolves the one-and-many problem with a single 'as if' — the chapter's metaphysical hinge.
verses.reflection: Watch many windows, one light, on your commute today — division as appearance, 'as if' divided.
verses.background: Krishna has shown the knowable both inside and outside beings, near and far. He now speaks of its presence among the many beings and of its part in their existence, which Śrīdhara assigns to the times of their maintenance, their dissolution and their creation.
verses.hook: How can the One seem divided among all beings yet stay whole?

refs.note: Time, karma, natures, living beings and matter are all the Lord himself; nothing exists apart from him, so he is undivided though he seems divided.

views.text: Like space, the Knowable stays the same in all beings; it only seems divided because it is perceived in separate bodies, as a rope seems a snake. It sustains beings while they last, devours them at dissolution, originates them at creation.

Reads the verse of the individual self: undivided because its form is that of the knower, yet appearing as god or man to the ignorant. It supports the body's elements, 'devours' food and turns it into blood, so it differs from the body.
Undivided as the cause, seemingly divided as the effects, like foam that is born from the sea and is never other than the sea.
Maps the three functions onto Brahmā who creates, Viṣṇu who sustains and Rudra who destroys; like fire hidden in wood, Brahman is hidden in every body.

All things are expansions of God's energy, so he seems divided among them yet stays whole, like the sun reflected in many puddles; like the ocean and its waves, he creates, sustains and withdraws the world.

verses.devanagari:
ज्योतिषामपि तज्ज्योतिस्तमसः परमुच्यते ।
ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं ज्ञानगम्यं हृदि सर्वस्य विष्ठितम्॥
verses.transliteration:
jyotiṣāmapi tajjyotistamasaḥ paramucyate
jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ jñānagamyaṃ hṛdi sarvasya viṣṭhitam
verses.essence: The light even of lights, it is called beyond darkness — knowledge, the knowable, the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of all.
verses.translation: That, the Light of all lights, is said to be beyond darkness: knowledge, the knowable and the goal of knowledge, seated in the hearts of all.

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + गम्य (to be reached): 'reachable by knowledge'

verses.explanation: The hymn's crown: jyotiṣām api taj jyotiḥ — the light by which all lights are light, the seeing behind every seen brightness. Then a triple identity that closes the circle of 13.1: the knowledge, the known, and knowing's destination are one. And the address, after all the cosmic sweep: hṛdi sarvasya — in everyone's heart. The farthest thing, filed under the nearest location.
verses.connection: Closes the jneya-hymn where every Gita teaching closes: in the heart — and 13.19 will say whose.
verses.reflection: Turn toward the light by which all your lights are lit — once, briefly, behind closed eyes.
verses.background: Śaṅkara raises the question that leads here: if the knowable is everywhere and yet unseen, is it then a kind of darkness? Krishna answers in the last verse of his description, speaking of its light and of where it is to be found.
verses.hook: What is the light that makes even the sun and stars shine?

refs.note: Everything shines after him; by his light all this is lit, so God is the light of lights.
By his radiance the sun and moon shine.

views.text: Sun and fire shine only as lit by the Self's consciousness. 'Beyond darkness' means untouched by ignorance. Knowledge, the knowable and the known are named together to cheer anyone who thinks knowledge too hard to reach.
Darkness (tamas) here means prakṛti in its subtle state; the self transcends it. Lamps only remove the darkness between eye and object, while the self's own light of knowledge is what reveals them.
'Seated in the heart' is read as standing there unshaken as the inner controller; the Light is reached through the means of knowledge listed earlier, humility and the rest.
As sunlight falls on everything but blazes in a clean mirror, Brahman is in all things yet shines with special brightness in a purified intellect.
The sun, moon and fire have no light of their own; God gives them their power to shine. He is also knowledge itself, what is to be known, and the goal of all knowing.

verses.devanagari:
इति क्षेत्रं तथा ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं चोक्तं समासतः ।
मद्भक्त एतद्विज्ञाय मद्भावायोपपद्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
iti kṣetraṃ tathā jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ coktaṃ samāsataḥ
madbhakta etadvijñāya madbhāvāyopapadyate
verses.essence: Thus the field, and knowledge, and the object of knowledge have been told in brief. My devotee, understanding this, becomes fit for my state of being.
verses.translation: Thus the field, as well as knowledge and the knowable have been briefly stated. My devotee, knowing this, enters into My Being.

anvaya.form: gerundive (to be known), neuter, nominative singular
past passive participle, neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: मद् (me) + भक्त (devotee): 'one devoted to me'
मद् (my) + भाव (state): 'my state of being'

verses.explanation: The section signs off, and the signature is devotional: not 'the philosopher' but mad-bhaktaḥ — *my devotee*, knowing this, grows into mad-bhāvāya, my way of being. The chapter's driest analysis was, all along, a love letter's enclosure: the metaphysics exists to make the union real, not the union to decorate the metaphysics.
verses.connection: Seals 13.2–18 and re-addresses it to the lover — then turns to prakriti and purusha.
verses.reflection: Let your study end as the section ends: knowledge folded into devotion, analysis into love.
verses.background: The description of the knowable is complete. Krishna now closes the whole section on the field, on knowledge and on the knowable. Śrīdhara notes that in closing he also names who is fit for this teaching and what it brings.
verses.hook: Who can truly understand this teaching, and what do they gain?

refs.note: Those who worship the Supreme Person without material desires pass beyond the cycle of birth and death.
The meaning of scripture shines in one who has supreme devotion to God and the same toward the Guru.
Devotion alone leads to God, shows him and brings one to him, for God is ruled by devotion.

views.text: The devotee is one who sees Vāsudeva as the Self of all, sure that whatever he sees, hears or touches is the Lord; understanding this, he becomes fit for the state of the supreme Self, liberation.
'My state of being' is the Lord's own nature taken as freedom from transmigration; the devotee who knows field, means and self becomes worthy of that freedom.
Reverses the order: whoever understands this triad of field, knowledge and knowable is, by that very understanding, the devotee, and attains the Lord's state.
The devotee meant is the one described in the previous chapter; knowing this summary, he becomes fit for Brahman-hood.
Only devotees truly grasp this knowledge, since devotion is the needed ingredient in every path; it not only reveals God but makes the devotee godlike, fit for his nature.

verses.devanagari:
प्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव विद्ध्यनादी उभावपि ।
विकारांश्च गुणांश्चैव विद्धि प्रकृतिसम्भवान्॥
verses.transliteration:
prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ caiva viddhyanādī ubhāvapi
vikārāṃśca guṇāṃścaiva viddhi prakṛtisambhavān
verses.essence: Know that prakriti and purusha are both beginningless; and know the modifications and the gunas as born of prakriti.
verses.translation: Know thou that Nature (matter) and the Spirit are both beginningless; and know also that all modifications and qualities are born of Nature.

anvaya.parts: अ (no) + आदि (beginning): 'having no beginning'
प्रकृति (nature) + सम्भव (origin): 'having nature as their source'

verses.explanation: The remaining pair from 13.1 taken up: matter and spirit, both anādī — neither created the other; they are co-eternal principles, older than any beginning. But everything that *changes* — every modification, every guna-weather — traces to prakriti's side alone. Eternity is shared; activity is not.
verses.connection: Opens the prakriti-purusha analysis (13.20–24): the field and knower under their classical names.
verses.reflection: Stop blaming spirit for matter's weather today — changes belong to prakriti; you watch them.
verses.background: Krishna has now shown what the field is and what it is like. Śrīdhara says he turns to the points promised at 13.4 still unanswered, the field's changes, its origin, and who the knower is and what his powers are, by treating nature (prakṛti) and spirit (puruṣa) over five verses.
verses.hook: Are matter and the soul created, or have they always existed?

refs.note: The soul is a fragment of God's soul energy, which supports calling the soul, like matter, an eternal energy of God.

views.text: Prakṛti and puruṣa are the two aspects of God through which He creates, sustains and dissolves; since His lordship is eternal, they too are beginningless. He rejects reading anādi as 'not the first cause'.
Both the binding modifications, desire and hatred, and the freeing qualities, modesty and the rest, arise from prakṛti; the same prakṛti that binds the self also brings its release.
If either had a beginning, another nature would be needed to produce it, without end. Prakṛti is beginningless as the Lord's power, the soul as His part.
The same teaching is now given in Sāṅkhya's terms of spirit and nature, but without accepting Sāṅkhya's dualism; like a mother feeding a child in small portions, Krishna teaches step by step.
Material nature and the soul are both eternal energies of God, one insentient and one conscious; the soul stays unchanged while matter brings about the body's changes and the three gunas.

verses.devanagari:
कार्यकारणकर्तृत्वे हेतुः प्रकृतिरुच्यते ।
पुरुषः सुखदुःखानां भोक्तृत्वे हेतुरुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
kāryakāraṇakartṛtve hetuḥ prakṛtirucyate
puruṣaḥ sukhaduḥkhānāṃ bhoktṛtve heturucyate
verses.essence: In the production of effect and cause, prakriti is said to be the cause; in the experiencing of pleasures and pains, purusha is said to be the cause.
verses.translation: In the production of the effect and the cause, Nature (matter) is said to be the cause; in the experience of pleasure and pain, the soul is said to be the cause.

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (in the matter of)
anvaya.parts: कार्य (effect, e.g. the body) + कारण (cause) + कर्तृत्व (agency): 'agency in producing effect and cause' (variant reading करण, 'instrument', the organs)
सुख (pleasure) + दुःख (pain): 'pleasures and pains' (a pair)

anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative singular (in the matter of)

verses.explanation: The division of labor: prakriti does all the *doing* — every body built, every instrument wielded, every effect produced — while purusha contributes exactly one thing: bhoktṛtva, the capacity to *experience* it. Nature acts and feels nothing; spirit acts not and feels everything. The whole drama requires both: a play, and an audience of one.
verses.connection: The job descriptions behind 13.2's field and knower — and the seam where 13.22's trouble starts.
verses.reflection: Honor the division of labor once today: nature does all the doing; you contribute the experiencing.
verses.background: Krishna has just said that nature and spirit are both beginningless and that all changes and qualities come from nature. Śaṅkara's question leads in: which are these changes and qualities? Krishna answers by giving nature and spirit their separate roles in a living being.
verses.hook: What does matter cause, and what is the soul responsible for?

refs.note: The world, though unreal, still causes suffering, like a dream of being beheaded that hurts until one wakes; so the soul suffers while it identifies with the body.

views.text: Kārya is the body and karaṇa the thirteen organs; nature is their source. He also allows the reading kāraṇa, 'cause'. Without nature's products and a conscious experiencer, there could be no worldly existence at all.
The operations of body and senses rest on prakṛti, yet the self is still an agent in the sense that it wills the effort to support the body, as the Brahma-sūtra says.
Insentient nature cannot act by itself; it acts in the presence of the conscious person, as milk flows for the calf; so nature's agency is spoken of because the person is near.
Matter, under Brahmā's plan, produces all bodies and their workings; the soul, identifying with body and mind as in a dream, experiences their pleasure and pain and so is held responsible.

verses.devanagari:
पुरुषः प्रकृतिस्थो हि भुङ्क्ते प्रकृतिजान्गुणान् ।
कारणं गुणसङ्गोऽस्य सदसद्योनिजन्मसु॥
verses.transliteration:
puruṣaḥ prakṛtistho hi bhuṅkte prakṛtijānguṇān
kāraṇaṃ guṇasaṅgo'sya sadasadyonijanmasu
verses.essence: For purusha, seated in prakriti, experiences the gunas born of prakriti. Attachment to the gunas is the cause of its births in good and evil wombs.
verses.translation: The soul seated in Nature experiences the qualities born of Nature; attachment to the qualities is the cause of its birth in good and evil wombs.

anvaya.parts: प्रकृति (nature) + स्थ (situated): 'situated in nature'
प्रकृति (nature) + ज (born): 'born from nature'
गुण (qualities) + सङ्ग (attachment): 'attachment to the qualities'

anvaya.meaning: of births in good and evil wombs
anvaya.form: noun, neuter, locative plural (in the matter of)
anvaya.parts: सत् (good) + असत् (evil) + योनि (womb) + जन्मन् (birth): 'births in good and evil wombs'

verses.explanation: The diagnosis of bondage in one compound: guṇa-saṅgaḥ — the audience leaning so far into the play that it forgets it has a seat. The watcher, prakriti-stha, embedded in nature, tastes her qualities and *identifies*; and that identification, nothing else, is what books the next womb. Rebirth is not a punishment; it is a season ticket the absorbed viewer keeps renewing.
verses.connection: Answers the oldest question — why is the free spirit bound? — with a single word: attachment.
verses.reflection: Catch one moment of leaning too far into the show today — and ease back into your seat.
verses.background: Krishna has said that spirit is the cause of experiencing pleasure and pain. Śrīdhara states the puzzle this leaves: how can a spirit that never changes and is never born be an experiencer at all? This verse answers, and also says what sends it into births high and low.
verses.hook: Why is the soul born again and again in higher or lower bodies?

views.text: 'Seated in nature' names ignorance, identifying with body and organs; 'attachment to the gunas' names desire. These two cause rebirth, and they are named so that knowledge and dispassion can remove them.
Attached to the pleasures of each body, the self does good and evil deeds and is reborn to reap them, a cycle that lasts as long as it does not cultivate modesty and the other means.
Takes guṇa-saṅga as contact with the senses, the 'qualities' that do good and bad deeds; that contact causes births among gods (good wombs) or animals (evil wombs).

Taking the body for itself, the soul seeks pleasure in the gunas and claims the body's acts as its own, like a driver answerable for a bus; the karma it gathers drives its rebirth in good and bad wombs.

verses.devanagari:
उपद्रष्टानुमन्ता च भर्ता भोक्ता महेश्वरः ।
परमात्मेति चाप्युक्तो देहेऽस्मिन्पुरुषः परः॥
verses.transliteration:
upadraṣṭānumantā ca bhartā bhoktā maheśvaraḥ
paramātmeti cāpyukto dehe'sminpuruṣaḥ paraḥ
verses.essence: The witness and the consenter, the supporter, the experiencer, the great Lord — and also called the supreme Self: thus is the highest purusha in this body.
verses.translation: The Supreme Soul in this body is also called the spectator, the permitter, the supporter, the enjoyer, the great Lord and the Supreme Self.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + ईश्वर (lord): 'the great Lord'
परम (supreme) + आत्मन् (self): 'the highest Self'

anvaya.form: past passive participle, masculine, nominative singular

verses.explanation: Six titles, rising in scope: upadraṣṭā, the close witness who watches without taking part; anumantā, the consenter who permits without compelling; bhartā, the supporter; bhoktā, the experiencer; maheśvara, the great Lord; and finally paramātmā, the supreme Self. The puruṣa that 13.22 showed entangled in nature is here called para, the highest, in this very body. Whether that is the same self seen truly or an inner Lord beside the soul is where the schools part; the verse itself insists only that the one in the body stands beyond what it watches.
verses.connection: The chapter's quiet revelation: the purusha in this very body is the highest — 13.3 made anatomical.
verses.reflection: Remember your closest companion today: the witness and consenter seated in this very body.
verses.background: Krishna has just traced the spirit's bondage to its seat in nature. Śrīdhara reads what follows as the other side: that bondage comes from confusing spirit with nature, not from what spirit is. So Krishna now names the supreme spirit present in this same body, by its many titles.
verses.hook: Who else lives in this body besides the individual soul?

refs.note: Two birds sit on one tree: the soul eats its fruits and grieves, while its friend the Lord only watches; when the soul turns to him, its sorrow ends.

views.text: Upadraṣṭā is like the expert priest who sits beside a sacrifice without acting and watches its merits and faults; anumantā approves and never dissuades the organs. All the titles describe the one Self, the innermost observer.
Every title belongs to the individual self: it watches, approves, supports and rules its own body, so it is 'great lord' and 'supreme self' only in relation to that body.
Nature and soul depend on each other like the lame and the blind; all of it, nature, its modifications and the soul, is beginningless because it is one with Brahman.
Though dwelling in the body, nature's product, the puruṣa is 'para', distinct and untouched by its qualities; the titles echo scripture's names for the inner controller and lord of beings.
Beside the soul in every body sits the Supreme Soul, a form of Vishnu, who witnesses its acts and gives their results; the soul's sorrow ends when it uses its free will to turn toward him.

verses.devanagari:
य एवं वेत्ति पुरुषं प्रकृतिं च गुणैः सह ।
सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि न स भूयोऽभिजायते॥
verses.transliteration:
ya evaṃ vetti puruṣaṃ prakṛtiṃ ca guṇaiḥ saha
sarvathā vartamāno'pi na sa bhūyo'bhijāyate
verses.essence: One who thus knows the purusha and prakriti together with the gunas — in whatever condition existing, that one is not born again.
verses.translation: He who thus knows the Spirit and Matter together with the qualities, in whatever condition he may be, he is not born again.
verses.explanation: The payoff clause, with the Gita's recurring generosity: sarvathā vartamāno 'pi — *however* such a knower happens to be living. Monk or monarch, battlefield or hermitage: once the seer, the seen, and the strands are correctly told apart, the womb-booking mechanism of 13.22 has nothing left to grip. Knowing this distinction *is* the exit.
verses.connection: Seals 13.20–23: right discrimination, in any lifestyle, ends rebirth.
verses.reflection: Apply the exemption clause to yourself: however you are living, right discrimination still frees.
verses.background: The supreme spirit in the body has just been named by its titles. Śaṅkara takes this verse as closing the explanation of 13.3, where Krishna called himself the knower in all fields, by stating what becomes of one who knows spirit and nature in this way.
verses.hook: What does knowing matter, soul and their gunas do for you?

refs.note: The Lord sustains the changing world and the changeless souls; the soul is bound by thinking itself the enjoyer, and knowing God frees it from every bond.

views.text: The knower knows the Person as 'I am That'. Knowledge burns up all his actions, as hundreds of Upaniṣadic texts say, so after this body falls he takes no other.
'In whatever condition' means in whatever painful state among gods or men; when this body falls, the knower reaches the pure self of boundless knowledge.
Praises discriminating knowledge: such a knower is freed even if he lives outside the rules of conduct.

Ignorance of its identity as a fragment of God has trapped the soul, so knowledge frees it; but this means realized wisdom, learned from the Guru and scripture and then lived out in spiritual practice.

verses.devanagari:
ध्यानेनात्मनि पश्यन्ति केचिदात्मानमात्मना ।
अन्ये साङ्ख्येन योगेन कर्मयोगेन चापरे॥
verses.transliteration:
dhyānenātmani paśyanti kecidātmānamātmanā
anye sāṅkhyena yogena karmayogena cāpare
verses.essence: By meditation some behold the Self in the self by the self; others by the yoga of knowledge, and others by the yoga of action.
verses.translation: Some by meditation behold the Self in the self by the self, others by the Yoga of knowledge, and still others by the Yoga of action.

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + योग (discipline): 'the discipline of action'

verses.explanation: Three doors to the one seeing: the meditator's stillness, the analyst's discrimination, the worker's consecrated action — chapters 6, 13, and 3 of this very book, listed as parallel entrances. The triple ātma in the first line is the destination's signature: the Self, seen in the self, by the self. Nothing external was ever required; only one of these ways of turning around.
verses.connection: Maps the Gita's own paths onto 13.24's liberating knowledge — and 13.26 adds a fourth door.
verses.reflection: Use your door today — stillness, analysis, or consecrated work — without envying the other doors.
verses.background: Krishna has promised freedom from rebirth to one who knows spirit and nature. Śrīdhara notes that he now gives, in two verses, the different means by which that knowledge of the self is reached, suited to different seekers. This first verse names three of them.
verses.hook: Are there different paths for different kinds of seekers?

refs.note: True knowledge is what turns the mind toward God; every path finds its fulfilment in devotion.

views.text: Meditation is an unbroken current of thought, like a stream of poured oil. The three ways are graded: the best seekers are fit for meditation, the middling for Sāṅkhya reflection, the rest for action dedicated to God.

Perfected yogis see the self by meditation, others by the path of knowledge; those unfit for it, or preferring an easier path, or great men like Janaka, use karma yoga, which already contains knowledge.

Takes sāṅkhya and yoga separately, discrimination of nature from spirit, and the eight-limbed yoga, so the means are alternatives fitted to each person's bent, though they can also be combined in sequence.
Souls differ, so some delight in meditation, some in the study of soul, God and matter, and some in service through action; each path is fulfilled when it is joined with devotion for God's pleasure.

verses.devanagari:
अन्ये त्वेवमजानन्तः श्रुत्वान्येभ्य उपासते ।
तेऽपि चातितरन्त्येव मृत्युं श्रुतिपरायणाः॥
verses.transliteration:
anye tvevamajānantaḥ śrutvānyebhya upāsate
te'pi cātitarantyeva mṛtyuṃ śrutiparāyaṇāḥ
verses.essence: Others again, not knowing thus, worship having heard from others; they too cross beyond death, devoted to what they have heard.
verses.translation: Others also, not knowing thus, worship, having heard of It from others; they, too, cross beyond death, regarding what they have heard as the Supreme refuge.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + जानन्त् (knowing): 'not knowing'
श्रुति (hearing) + परायण (supreme refuge): 'those for whom hearing is the highest resort'

verses.explanation: The door for everyone else, and it may be the warmest verse in the chapter: those without the meditation, the philosophy, or the discipline — who simply *heard* the truth from someone and trusted it — te 'pi ca atitaranty eva, they also cross, emphatically. Śruti-parāyaṇāḥ: holding to the heard. A grandmother's faith and a scholar's realization arrive at the same far shore.
verses.connection: Completes 13.25's map with the path of trusting ears — no one is left outside the count.
verses.reflection: If all you have is trust in what you heard — use it fully today; the hearers also cross.
verses.background: Three ways to see the self have just been named: meditation, knowledge and action. Śrīdhara says this verse gives a way across for the least prepared seekers, those who cannot follow any of these paths on their own.
verses.hook: Can those who only hear the teaching from others also cross beyond death?

refs.note: Krishna, dwelling in the heart, cleanses the impurities of those who hear about him, so simply hearing from saints purifies.

views.text: These are people without discrimination of their own who take their teachers' word as authority and reflect on it with faith; if even they cross death, the discriminating cross all the more.
Hearing comes first: listening to those who know, they later take up karma yoga and the rest and so pass beyond death. The word 'too' marks a difference in level.
The point is that the Bhagavat, reflected on by any means at all, carries one across the cycle of birth and death, so one should keep to it somehow.
Most people come to the path by hearing from others; hearing from saints gives true knowledge and passes on their faith and enthusiasm, the foundations of devotion.

verses.devanagari:
यावत्सञ्जायते किञ्चित्सत्त्वं स्थावरजङ्गमम् ।
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञसंयोगात्तद्विद्धि भरतर्षभ॥
verses.transliteration:
yāvatsañjāyate kiñcitsattvaṃ sthāvarajaṅgamam
kṣetrakṣetrajñasaṃyogāttadviddhi bharatarṣabha
verses.essence: Whatever being is born, moving or unmoving — know it, best of Bharatas, to be from the union of field and field-knower.
verses.translation: Wherever a being is born, whether unmoving or moving, know thou, O best of the Bharatas (Arjuna), that it is from the union between the field and its knower.

anvaya.parts: स्थावर (unmoving) + जङ्गम (moving): 'whether stationary or moving' (a pair)

anvaya.meaning: from union of field and knower
anvaya.parts: क्षेत्र (field) + क्षेत्रज्ञ (knower of the field) + संयोग (union): 'from the union of the field and its knower'
भरत (Bharata's line) + ऋषभ (bull): 'bull among the Bharatas'

verses.explanation: A universal birth-formula: every existent thing — blade of grass, tiger, god — arises from saṃyoga, the joining of field and field-knower. Matter alone would be dark; spirit alone would produce nothing; whatever is born is the two taken together. What kind of joining this is, the commentators debate: for Śaṅkara it is a mistaken superimposition of each on the other, undone by knowledge; for Rāmānuja every being is simply born as a compound of the two. Either way, nothing comes into being from one side alone.
verses.connection: Generalizes the body-analysis of 13.2 to all of existence — preparing the equal vision of 13.28.
verses.reflection: See one birth or beginning today as the meeting of two: matter shaped, spirit witnessing.
verses.background: With the paths to self-knowledge mapped, Śrīdhara notes that action and meditation were treated in earlier chapters, so Krishna spends the rest of this one on telling spirit apart from nature. He begins with how every creature, moving or unmoving, comes to be born.
verses.hook: Where does every living being, moving or still, come from?

views.text: Field and knower, object and subject, cannot touch like rope and pot; their 'union' is mutual superimposition, like a snake seen on a rope. Seeing the field as unreal as a dream ends it, and with it rebirth.
Every being, moving or still, is born only as a compound of body and self, never as either one separately.
Whatever exists is born not as something altogether different from the field and its knower.
Every form of life, however large or small, joins a soul to a body of matter; wherever there is consciousness there is a soul, so plants and animals have souls too.

verses.devanagari:
समं सर्वेषु भूतेषु तिष्ठन्तं परमेश्वरम् ।
विनश्यत्स्वविनश्यन्तं यः पश्यति स पश्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
samaṃ sarveṣu bhūteṣu tiṣṭhantaṃ parameśvaram
vinaśyatsvavinaśyantaṃ yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati
verses.essence: One who sees the supreme Lord standing equally in all beings — the undying within the dying — that one truly sees.
verses.translation: He sees, who sees the Supreme Lord, existing equally in all beings, the unperishing within the perishing.

anvaya.parts: परम (supreme) + ईश्वर (lord): 'the highest Lord'
अ (not) + विनश्यन्त् (perishing): 'not perishing'

verses.explanation: The chapter's crowning verse, sealed with the Gita's favorite construction: yaḥ paśyati sa paśyati — whoever sees this, *sees*; all other seeing is preliminary. The content of true sight: the same Lord, samam, in every being without exception, the avinaśyat standing calm inside everything that is visibly dying. To look at any perishing creature and perceive the imperishable in it — that is the eye this whole chapter has been building, and once it is trained, every encounter becomes darshan.
verses.connection: The vision-test of the chapter: 13.27's universal union perceived as the one Lord in all.
verses.reflection: Take the seeing-test once: find the undying in something visibly aging — a parent, a tree, yourself.
verses.background: Krishna has just said every creature is born from the joining of field and knower, which Śrīdhara reads as a confusion of the two. To end that confusion, Krishna now describes right seeing, the vision of one who truly sees.
verses.hook: What does it mean to truly see?

refs.note: The one God lies hidden in all beings, pervading everything as the inner Self of all.
God dwells in all beings as their Self, the witness and master.
Lord Rāma is eternal and beyond all, yet dwells in the heart of every being.

views.text: 'Imperishable among the perishing' shows the Lord's total difference from changing beings. Others see too, but wrongly, like a man with an eye disease who sees many moons; only one who sees the one undivided Self truly sees.
The true seer sees the self as the same imperishable ruler in every body, god or man; whoever sees it as shaped by those bodies, born and dying, stays bound in transmigration.
Heat is the same in every fire and gold the same in every ornament; so the one Self is the same in ant and elephant, king and beggar, saint and rogue.
Seeing the soul in the body is not enough; true seeing recognizes God, the Supreme Soul, seated in every body, who travels with the soul from life to life.

verses.devanagari:
समं पश्यन्हि सर्वत्र समवस्थितमीश्वरम् ।
न हिनस्त्यात्मनात्मानं ततो याति परां गतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
samaṃ paśyanhi sarvatra samavasthitamīśvaram
na hinastyātmanātmānaṃ tato yāti parāṃ gatim
verses.essence: For, seeing the Lord equally present everywhere, one does not injure the Self by the self — and so reaches the supreme goal.
verses.translation: Because he who sees the same Lord equally dwelling everywhere does not destroy the Self by the self; he goes to the highest goal.
verses.explanation: The fruit of the vision: na hinasti ātmanā ātmānam — one no longer injures the Self by the self. The commentators take this inward first: whoever mistakes the body for the Self keeps 'killing' himself, dropping one body and taking up another, his true Self as good as lost to ignorance. Seeing the same Lord evenly present everywhere ends that self-injury, and so one reaches the highest goal. An outward corollary follows naturally — if the same Lord lives in every being, harming another is harming oneself — but the verse's own point is liberation.
verses.connection: Turns 13.28's perception into its fruit: no more self-injury through ignorance, and the highest goal.
verses.reflection: Let equal vision do its quiet work today: whom could you injure, seeing the same Lord there?
verses.background: Krishna has just said that only one who sees the supreme Lord equally in all beings truly sees. Śrīdhara takes this verse as the answer to the question that follows: why is that seeing so decisive?
verses.hook: How does seeing God in everyone change the way you live?

views.text: The ignorant all 'destroy the Self': they take a non-Self for the Self, drop it at death, take up another, and leave the real Self as if lost. The knower of the one Lord injures it in neither way and reaches liberation.
Seeing every self as the same form of knowledge, free of the shapes of god or man, one does not 'injure' the self by the mind; seeing it as the body hurls it into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Not injuring means not obscuring, through ignorance, the Self whose nature is being, consciousness and bliss; he cites the Upaniṣad on 'self-slayers' who go to sunless worlds.

Seeing God in all beings guides the mind through the intellect: one stops using others for gain, respects and serves everyone, drops human divisions of caste, creed and status, and so reaches the goal.

verses.devanagari:
प्रकृत्यैव च कर्माणि क्रियमाणानि सर्वशः ।
यः पश्यति तथात्मानमकर्तारं स पश्यति॥
verses.transliteration:
prakṛtyaiva ca karmāṇi kriyamāṇāni sarvaśaḥ
yaḥ paśyati tathātmānamakartāraṃ sa paśyati
verses.essence: And one who sees that actions are performed everywhere by prakriti alone, and likewise that the Self is not the doer — that one truly sees.
verses.translation: He sees, who sees that all actions are performed by Nature alone and that the Self is actionless.

anvaya.form: present passive participle, neuter, accusative plural

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कर्तृ (doer): 'one who is not the doer'

verses.explanation: The second seeing-test: all activity, sarvaśaḥ, credited to nature's account; the Self standing as akartā, the non-doer — 3.27's teaching now part of liberating vision itself. Watch any action closely enough — a hand moving, a thought forming — and find machinery operating and a witness present, with no third party doing. The doer was always a misreading.
verses.connection: Pairs with 13.28 as the chapter's twin visions: the Lord in all, the Self in none of the doing.
verses.reflection: Watch one action closely today — machinery operating, witness present, no third party doing.
