verses.background: Krishna has claimed the same Lord is present equally everywhere. Śrīdhara voices the objection this meets: people plainly differ by their good and bad deeds, so how can the self be the same in all? The answer turns to who really does those deeds.
verses.hook: Who really does your actions, the body or the self?

refs.note: The soul is caught in worldly existence by the ego of being the body and the doer.
Vasiṣṭha tells Rāma to act outwardly as if results depend on him, but inwardly know himself as not the doer.

views.text: The nature meant is God's māyā of three qualities, not Sāṅkhya's independent pradhāna; the Self is a non-agent free of every adjunct, with no real differences in it, like space.

The self, whose form is knowledge, is not the doer; its tie to prakṛti, its directing of the body and its pleasures and pains come from ignorance in the form of karma. Seeing this is seeing the pure self.
The one with the firm conviction 'nature does all this, I do nothing' does nothing in truth, even while doing everything.
Answers an objection: deeds differ, so how is the Self the same everywhere? Doership belongs to it only through identifying with the body, never by its own nature.
The enlightened soul sees that the body acts, not the self, yet still accepts responsibility for those acts, as a president answers for a war he does not fight; one keeps both truths in view.

verses.devanagari:
यदा भूतपृथग्भावमेकस्थमनुपश्यति ।
तत एव च विस्तारं ब्रह्म सम्पद्यते तदा॥
verses.transliteration:
yadā bhūtapṛthagbhāvamekasthamanupaśyati
tata eva ca vistāraṃ brahma sampadyate tadā
verses.essence: When one perceives the separate existence of beings as resting in the One, and their expansion from That alone — then one attains Brahman.
verses.translation: When a man sees the whole variety of beings as resting in the One, and spreading forth from That alone, he then becomes Brahman.

anvaya.parts: भूत (beings) + पृथक् (separate) + भाव (state): 'the separate existence of beings'
एक (one) + स्थ (situated): 'abiding in the One'

verses.explanation: The vision in motion, both directions at once: all multiplicity seen folding back into one ground, and the whole spread of things seen pouring out from it — the ocean in the waves, the waves from the ocean. Brahma sampadyate: at that seeing, one does not travel to Brahman; one *amounts to* it. The arrival is the perception.
verses.connection: The unitive climax of the three visions (13.28, 13.30, 13.31): diversity read as one substance unfolding.
verses.reflection: Trace the many back to the One once today, and the One out into the many — both directions, one look.
verses.background: Two marks of the true seer have been given: seeing the Lord equal in all beings, and seeing nature as the doer of all action. Śaṅkara says Krishna now states the same knowledge once more in other words, this time about the many separate beings themselves.
verses.hook: What unity lies behind the endless variety of beings?

views.text: Realizing in direct experience that 'all this is the Self', one sees every distinction among beings resting in the one Self and arising from it, as the Chāndogya says life, space and food come from the Self; then one is Brahman.

The 'one' in which beings' differences rest is prakṛti, not the self: tall or short, divine or human, and all their offspring spring from prakṛti alone. Seeing this, one attains the self in its pure form.

Diversity rests in prakṛti, the Lord's power, at dissolution and spreads from it at creation; seeing beings as nothing but prakṛti, one no longer sees the Self divided by them and becomes the full Brahman.
Like waves and foam that are all ocean, all beings are souls in bodies made of the same material nature; seeing this unity, and nature as God's energy, leads to the realization of Brahman.

verses.devanagari:
अनादित्वान्निर्गुणत्वात्परमात्मायमव्ययः ।
शरीरस्थोऽपि कौन्तेय न करोति न लिप्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
anāditvānnirguṇatvātparamātmāyamavyayaḥ
śarīrastho'pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate
verses.essence: Being without beginning and without gunas, this imperishable supreme Self, though dwelling in the body, Kaunteya, neither acts nor is stained.
verses.translation: Being without beginning and being devoid of (any) qualities, the Supreme Self, imperishable, though dwelling in the body, O Arjuna, neither acts nor is tainted.

anvaya.parts: अ (no) + आदि (beginning) + त्व (-ness): 'having no beginning'
निर् (without) + गुण (qualities) + त्व (-ness): 'being without qualities'
परम (supreme) + आत्मन् (self): 'the highest Self'
अ (not) + व्यय (decay): 'not subject to decay'
शरीर (body) + स्थ (situated): 'abiding in the body'

verses.explanation: The residency clause: śarīra-stho 'pi — *even while in the body*, the supreme Self does nothing and catches nothing. The logic is given, not just asserted: having no beginning, it never entered the causal stream; having no gunas, it offers karma no surface to adhere to. Two similes now follow to make the untouchability visible.
verses.connection: States the immunity that 13.33–34 will illustrate with space and sun.
verses.reflection: Carry the immunity clause through a messy day: dwelling in it all, doing none of it, stained by none.
verses.background: If one Self dwells in all bodies, Śaṅkara asks, does it not share their faults? The doubt is sharp, since the Self seems caught up in each body's deeds and in the pleasures and pains they bring; Krishna answers it here.
verses.hook: Why is the Supreme Self untouched though it dwells in the body?

views.text: What has no cause has no parts and loses nothing; what has no qualities cannot perish by losing them. If the Self does not act, who does? Nature, which is ignorance, as 5.14 says; in the Self itself no action occurs.
The self, defined as other than the body, is never created and so does not decay; being free of prakṛti's gunas, it neither acts nor is tainted by the body's qualities.

Meets a doubt: if pleasure and pain differ from body to body, how can vision be equal? Whatever is born or has qualities decays; this Self has neither, so it is changeless and the fruits of action do not stain it.
God, seated in the heart as the Supreme Soul, never identifies with the body and is not made material by being there, nor bound by karma or by birth and death, which the soul goes through.

verses.devanagari:
यथा सर्वगतं सौक्ष्म्यादाकाशं नोपलिप्यते ।
सर्वत्रावस्थितो देहे तथात्मा नोपलिप्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yathā sarvagataṃ saukṣmyādākāśaṃ nopalipyate
sarvatrāvasthito dehe tathātmā nopalipyate
verses.essence: As the all-pervading space, by its subtlety, is not stained — so the Self, present everywhere in the body, is not stained.
verses.translation: As the all-pervading ether is not tainted, because of its subtlety, so the Self seated everywhere in the body is not tainted.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (everywhere) + गत (gone): 'gone everywhere, all-pervading'

verses.explanation: The first simile: ākāśa, space — present in the sewer and the shrine equally, dirtied by neither, because its subtlety gives filth nothing to land on. So the Self in the body: host to every process, participant in none. Whatever the body and mind have done or suffered, the space they happened *in* remains exactly as clean as before any of it.
verses.connection: Illustrates 13.32's non-staining: omnipresence without contamination.
verses.reflection: Be like space in one difficult room today: fully present, hosting everything, dirtied by nothing.
verses.background: Krishna has just said the supreme Self neither acts nor is stained, though it lives in the body. Śaṅkara says he now gives an illustration to show how something can be present and yet untouched.
verses.hook: How can the Self live in the body and stay unstained?

views.text: Space, though all-pervading, is not defiled and does not come into contact with things, because of its subtlety; likewise the Self, present everywhere in the body, is not defiled.
Space touches every substance yet takes on none of their qualities; so the self, present in every body of god or man, is not contaminated by them, because it is extremely subtle.
Space stays clean even in mud because it does not cling; so the Self, whether in a high, middling or low body, is not touched by that body's merits or defects.
Like space, which holds everything but is subtler than what it holds and so stays untouched, the soul is a subtler energy and keeps its divine nature even while it identifies with the body.

verses.devanagari:
यथा प्रकाशयत्येकः कृत्स्नं लोकमिमं रविः ।
क्षेत्रं क्षेत्री तथा कृत्स्नं प्रकाशयति भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
yathā prakāśayatyekaḥ kṛtsnaṃ lokamimaṃ raviḥ
kṣetraṃ kṣetrī tathā kṛtsnaṃ prakāśayati bhārata
verses.essence: As the one sun illumines this entire world — so the owner of the field illumines the entire field, Bharata.
verses.translation: Just as the one sun illumines the whole world, so also the Lord of the field (Supreme Self) illumines the whole field, O Arjuna.

anvaya.base: प्र-√काश् · to shine; causative: to make shine
क्षेत्रिन् · one who has the field
प्र-√काश् · to shine; causative: to make shine

verses.explanation: The second simile answers the lingering 'but what does the non-doer *do*?': it shines. Ekaḥ raviḥ — one sun, the whole world lit; one kṣetrī, the entire field of body-mind made knowable. Illumination is not an action among actions; the sun ripens crops and bleaches bones without lifting a finger. Consciousness works exactly so: everything happens by its light, nothing by its hand.
verses.connection: The chapter's final image: the knower's whole relationship to the field — pure, effortless lighting.
verses.reflection: Illumine without managing once today — be the sun to a situation: light it, and let it ripen itself.
verses.background: The image of space has shown the Self untouched by the body it fills. Śrīdhara says a second image follows to make a further point: what gives light is not affected by the qualities of what it lights.
verses.hook: How can one small self give life and light to a whole body?

refs.note: Says the soul is exceedingly tiny, yet the verse shows it lights up the entire body with consciousness.
Puts the soul's size at a ten-thousandth of a hair's tip and says such souls are countless.
Though seated in the heart, the soul spreads its consciousness through the whole body, as the sun's light fills the world.

views.text: The sun image makes two points: like the sun, the Self is one in all fields, and like the sun, it remains unaffected by what it lights.
The knower lights up its body from head to foot by its own knowledge, 'this body of mine is such'; being the knower, it is as different from the body as the sun from the world it lights.
The space image showed that the Self is not stained because it does not cling; the sun image shows that whatever illumines does not take on the qualities of what it illumines.
The soul is minute, yet like the sun lighting the whole world from one place, it pervades the entire body with consciousness from its seat in the heart.

verses.devanagari:
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञयोरेवमन्तरं ज्ञानचक्षुषा ।
भूतप्रकृतिमोक्षं च ये विदुर्यान्ति ते परम्॥
verses.transliteration:
kṣetrakṣetrajñayorevamantaraṃ jñānacakṣuṣā
bhūtaprakṛtimokṣaṃ ca ye viduryānti te param
verses.essence: Those who, by the eye of knowledge, thus discern the distinction between field and field-knower, and the release of beings from prakriti — they go to the Supreme.
verses.translation: They who, by the eye of knowledge, perceive the distinction between the field and its knower and also the liberation from the Nature of being, go to the Supreme.

anvaya.base: क्षेत्र · field; क्षेत्रज्ञ · knower of the field
anvaya.form: noun, masculine, genitive dual (of the two)
anvaya.parts: क्षेत्र (field) + क्षेत्रज्ञ (knower of the field): 'the field and the field-knower' (a pair)
ज्ञान (knowledge) + चक्षुस् (eye): 'the eye that is knowledge'

anvaya.meaning: release from the nature of beings
anvaya.parts: भूत (beings) + प्रकृति (nature) + मोक्ष (release): 'release from the nature that makes up beings'

anvaya.form: verb, perfect with present sense, 3rd person plural
adjective used as noun, accusative singular (object)

verses.explanation: The chapter closes on its own instrument: jñāna-cakṣuṣā, the eye of knowledge — counterpart to the divine eye of 11.8, but this one is grown, not granted, through the twenty marks of 13.8–12. What it discerns is one antaram, one distinction — seer from seen — and with it bhūta-prakṛti-mokṣa, the way out of prakriti's whole machinery. The Gita's most analytic chapter ends having taught a single cut, and called it the door: yānti te param, those who see it go to the Supreme.
verses.connection: Seals the chapter: the field-knower distinction, truly seen, is itself the passage to the Supreme.
verses.reflection: Sharpen the one distinction before sleep: seer from seen — the single cut this chapter calls the door.
verses.background: The images of space and sun are done. In this final verse of chapter 13, Krishna draws the teaching on field and knower, begun at Arjuna's question, to a close. Śaṅkara calls it the summary of the whole chapter.
verses.hook: What do the wise gain by seeing body and knower as distinct?

views.text: Bhūta-prakṛti is ignorance, the Unmanifest that is the matrix of beings, and mokṣa is its annihilation; knowing this with the eye of Self-knowledge, they reach Brahman and take no body again.

Mokṣa here means the means of deliverance: modesty and the other virtues taught earlier. Knowing the difference of body and self and practising those virtues, they reach the self of infinite knowledge.
The eye is discriminative knowledge; the 'release' known is the means of release from prakṛti, meditation and the rest, and with both they reach the highest state.

Knowing the difference between the material field and the spiritual knower, the wise stop identifying with the body, see themselves as tiny parts of God, and walk the path that ends in God-realization.
